title: Day 44 · Week 6, Day 2 — Physiology: her heart is already running faster — the pump, the blood, the breath, the heart-rate limit retired in 1994, and the real size of two hundred milligrams
summary: The third Physiology episode, promised on Day 43. Your baby is 4–6 mm at the end of Carnegie stage 13 (NHS: a pea), the heart looped and dividing; stage 14 and the lens pits begin tomorrow. Her cardiovascular rebuild happened before anything showed: heart rate up from 2–5 weeks (Hunter & Robson 1992; +8 bpm by 8 weeks in Clapp 1985), cardiac output significantly higher by 5 weeks LMP and 4.88 → 7.21 L/min by 32 weeks in 13 women (Robson 1989), +1 L/min by 8 weeks and vascular resistance at 70% of baseline (Capeless & Clapp 1989), a +31% peak in the early third trimester pooled over 39 studies (Meah 2016), plasma volume +50% (Pritchard 1965; Soma-Pillay 2016), and the reference curves from 36,000 women — systolic lowest at 10 weeks (110), diastolic at 21 weeks (66), heart rate 79 → 87 (Loerup 2019) — which explain the dizziness. The breath: minute ventilation up to +48% from the first trimester via tidal volume, PaCO2 ~30 mmHg, oxygen consumption +20%, breathlessness in ~70% of healthy pregnant women (LoMauro & Aliverti 2015). Then the heart-rate myth: ACOG's 1985 ceiling of 140 bpm and 15 minutes, withdrawn in 1994, still given by 62% of surveyed obstetricians in 2006 and invoked in 69% of discussions in 2005 (Entin & Munhall 2006; Krans 2005); what replaced it — ≥150 min/week she can talk through (ACOG CO 804; Mottola 2018) — and the evidence under it: GDM −38%, gestational hypertension −39%, pre-eclampsia −41% in RCTs of 273,182 women (Davenport 2018), miscarriage OR 0.88 and perinatal death OR 0.86 in 266,778 women (Davenport 2019), reassuring fetal Dopplers after peak treadmill tests (Szymanski & Satin 2012), the Day 39 heat limits, and the real exclusions. Then caffeine: half-life 3.4 → 8.3 h in pregnancy and 10.5 h near term (Knutti 1981/82), what is actually in the cup (FDA 113–247 mg per 12 oz brewed; NHS 100/75/40/80), the 200 mg ceiling (ACOG CO 462; NHS), the one RCT (1,197 women, −182 mg/day, no effect: Cochrane 2015), Weng 2008's aHR 2.23 at ≥200 mg against Savitz 2008's null with visible recall bias, Chen 2016's dose-response (RR 1.02 at 50–149 mg, 1.40 at 350–699, 1.72 at ≥700; +7% per 100 mg; 130,456 women), the nausea confounder, CARE 2008's growth-restriction trend (OR 1.5 at 200–299 mg; 2,635 women), and Hinkle 2021's reminder that 41% of American women drink none and under 1% exceed 200.
action: Tonight, the caffeine audit, ten minutes: list everything with caffeine your partner had today and put a number beside each (instant ~100 mg a mug; coffee-shop coffee 150–300, look it up by brand and size; tea 75; cola 40; energy drink 80; dark chocolate 25). If the total is over 200 mg, she picks which one goes and you make it happen — buy decaf tomorrow for the second cup. If under, write the number on a card by the kettle so it stays under when the sickness lifts. Then one sentence to her about the stairs: it's the hormone, not her. And if anyone quotes 140 bpm, the answer is 'that was withdrawn in 1994; the rule is that she can talk.'
